title: One More Kick, Ella!
description: A 16-page Healthy Little Minds audiobook about comparing less, practicing more, and learning to keep growing.

pages.text: Hello, friend. Today, we're going to meet a girl named Ella. Ella is eight years old. She lives in Korea. And three times every week, she goes to Taekwondo academy. Ella loves Taekwondo. But one day, something happened that made her wonder if she should quit. Let's begin.

Every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, Ella packed her Taekwondo bag. She carefully folded her uniform. She checked that her belt was inside. Then she hurried to the academy. She never wanted to be late. Practice day was one of her favorite days of the week.

Ella loved Taekwondo. She loved learning new kicks. She loved practicing her forms. She loved bowing respectfully before class. And she especially loved shouting loudly during practice. "Kiyah!" It made her feel strong. It made her feel brave. It made her feel proud.

One Friday evening, the class was learning a new pattern.

Master Lee demonstrated each movement carefully.

Step.

Turn.

Block.

Kick.

Turn.

Block.

Kick.

The movements looked easy when Master Lee did them.

But they felt much harder when Ella tried.

Ella stepped forward.

She tried to follow the pattern.

Step.

Turn.

Block.

Then she forgot what came next.

She stopped.

She tried again.

And forgot again.

The student beside her finished perfectly.

Another student received praise from Master Lee.

Ella felt her shoulders sink.

As practice continued, Ella watched the other students.

Some kicked higher.

Some moved faster.

Some remembered every step.

Ella began comparing herself to them.

A quiet thought entered her mind.

"What if I'm not good enough?"

The thought stayed with her for the rest of practice.

That evening, Ella sat quietly during dinner.

Usually she talked about Taekwondo.

Usually she smiled.

Usually she laughed.

But tonight was different.

Her mother noticed.

"Ella, is something bothering you?"

Ella looked down at her rice bowl.

"I don't think I'm very good at Taekwondo."

Her mother listened carefully.

Then she asked,

"Do you remember your first day at Taekwondo?"

Ella nodded.

"You couldn't tie your belt by yourself."

Ella giggled.

"That's true."

"And now?"

"I can tie it really fast."

Her mother smiled.

"Do you remember when you were scared to perform in front of everyone?"

Ella nodded again.

"And now?"

"I can do that too."

Her mother gently placed a hand on Ella's shoulder.

"Ella, you're looking at students who have practiced for years."

"Instead of comparing yourself to them, compare yourself to the Ella you were before."

Ella thought quietly.

The Ella from before couldn't tie her belt.

The Ella from before was afraid to perform.

The Ella from before didn't know many patterns.

Maybe she had grown more than she realized.

The next Monday, Ella returned to the academy.

The pattern was still difficult.

She still forgot some movements.

She still made mistakes.

But this time, something felt different.

Instead of feeling embarrassed, she reminded herself,

"I'm learning."

And then she tried again.

Ella practiced every week.

Monday.

Wednesday.

Friday.

Little by little, the movements became easier.

Her turns became smoother.

Her kicks became stronger.

Her balance improved.

Not because she was perfect.

But because she kept showing up.

Several weeks later, Master Lee gathered the class.

Today, each student would demonstrate the pattern.

Ella felt butterflies in her stomach.

She took a deep breath.

Then she stepped forward.

The room became quiet.

Step.

Turn.

Block.

Kick.

Turn.

Block.

Kick.

This time, she remembered every movement.

When Ella finished, the room erupted with applause.

Master Lee smiled proudly.

"Excellent work, Ella."

Ella smiled too.

Not because she was the best student.

Not because she was perfect.

But because she had not given up.

That day, Ella learned something important.

Everyone learns at a different speed.

Everyone starts somewhere.

The goal isn't to be better than everyone else.

The goal is to keep growing.

One step.

One practice.

One day at a time.

Now it's your turn to think.

Have you ever tried something difficult?

Maybe a sport.

Maybe music.

Maybe reading.

Maybe something at school.

Did you make mistakes?

That's okay.

Mistakes are part of learning.

Every expert was once a beginner.

Every strong person started with a first step.

And every big achievement begins when we decide to keep trying.

Ella still goes to Taekwondo academy three times every week.

Sometimes practice is easy.

Sometimes practice is hard.

Sometimes she succeeds.

Sometimes she makes mistakes.

But now she knows something important.

Every time she tries again, she grows stronger.

Thank you for listening to One More Kick, Ella!

Until next time, keep learning.

Keep growing.

And keep believing in yourself.
